proposals.hypothesis: LiBr is a wide-gap halide insulator with no reducible cation. Its Br- anion is close in chemistry to the Cl- in Li6PS5Cl, so halide exchange at the sulfide contact should be mild. Earlier oxide, fluoride, chloride and borate coatings all released S, P or anion-exchange products, so a simple Li-halide tests a different contact chemistry. Br- is somewhat easier to oxidize than F- or Cl-, so the 4.0 V stability against LiCoO2 is the main risk.
proposals.motivation: Every oxide, fluoride, chloride and borate tried so far (best Li2O at penalty 0.189) failed the contact penalty through S/P/Cl-release reactions with Li6PS5Cl. None of the tested families was a simple Li-halide with a halide matching the electrolyte, so LiBr is the next family to test.

proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap (about 5 eV) electronic insulator with a high oxidation limit, so it should block electron transfer and resist oxidation at the LiCoO2 interface at 4.0 V. It is a well-known protective coating for oxide cathodes against sulfide electrolytes.

LiF is a very wide-gap, electrochemically robust insulator with a highly oxidized fluoride anion that should not be oxidized at 4.0 V. Its Li-F bonds are very strong, so it should be thermodynamically unlikely to react with the sulfide electrolyte. The Li3PO4 result showed that P-O-containing coatings can release sulfur and phosphorus oxide products at the sulfide contact, so a fluoride with no reducible sulfur-compatible cation should give a smaller contact penalty.

proposal.hypothesis: Li2MgCl4 is a wide-gap chloride insulator whose anion matches the Cl in Li6PS5Cl, so it should avoid the anion-exchange and sulfur-release reactions seen for the P-O and F-containing coatings.
